newsitem.title: UK: Irish guerrillas threaten Protestant politicians.
newsitem.headline: Irish guerrillas threaten Protestant politicians.

text.p: Left-wing republican guerrillas in Northern Ireland, angered by the killing of a Roman Catholic father of nine in Belfast, issued a warning on Saturday to Protestant politicians to stay out of Catholic areas.

"All our units have been informed of this decision and it will be rigorously enforced," the Irish National Liberation Army (INLA), a small group with ruthless record during decades of strife against British rule, said in a rare statement.

Earlier, David Ervine, a political ally of one of four banned Protestant guerrilla groups in the Combined Loyalist Military Command (CLMC), denied that pro-British units were behind the latest killing in Northern Ireland.

Sinn Fein, the political wing of the outlawed Irish Republican Army (IRA) fighting British rule in the province, blamed Loyalist guerrillas and said the murder was evidence that a shaky 29-month Loyalist ceasefire had ended.

"I am as much in the dark as anyone in terms of who has actually caused the murder of this gentleman last evening," Ervine told reporters. "However on numerous phone calls that I have made throughout the night and this morning I am fairly convinced that the Combined Loyalist Military Command are not responsible."

But he said it was possible maverick Loyalists might have shot John Slane, 44, in his west Belfast home. "That's a possiblity, I think we have got to wait and see. It certainly is a possibility and that must cause consternation to us all," he said.
Police said Slane was a guerrilla victim but they refused to speculate on which shadowy group pulled the trigger.
Saturday's INLA statement was issued about 15 hours after the attack on Slane.
"The Irish National Liberation Army remain committed to the principle of working-class unity and has not decided upon this action lightly," it said.

Accusing some Protestants of taking advantage of a 17-month lull in republican guerrilla violence to gather intelligence in Catholic areas where residents oppose British rule, the INLA said the murder victim's blood was "on their hands".

"This situation will no longer be tolerated. From today no representatives of the fringe loyalist or unionist parties can be permitted to participate in activities or functions based within Nationalist areas. Their unhindered sight seeing' tours will also stop," the statement said.
"This statement should not be misconstrued as a threat against Protestants genuinely involved in cross-community (Protestant and Catholic) work," it added.

Apparently referring to disclosures in a recent Belfast court case, the statement said that last week a list of "potential nationalist targets", which the INLA said had been compiled by the outlawed Protestant Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) had been found in a Loyalist stronghold of south Belfast.
The UVF is one of the pro-British Protestant guerrilla groups still honouring two-year-old ceasefires in their battle to keep Northern Ireland British.

The statement said that after the IRA declaration of a ceasefire in September, 1994, there had been what it described as a welcome increase in involvement by pro-British "representatives of the Unionist and Loyalist tradition" in joint activities with Irish Catholics to improve living standards.
But the INLA said it had reached the conclusion many months ago that their involvement was "not genuine".
The IRA abandoned its truce 13 months ago and relaunched a series of attacks on British targets. Loyalists say their ceasefire is intact despite several attacks blamed on renegade hardliners.
The INLA put its members on a war-footing last year but has kept a low profile, according to security analysts.

The group was responsible for a wave of killings and bombings aimed at British security forces and prominent politicians, in a bid to force an end to British rule. Several members were shot in an internal power struggle last year.
The Protestant guerrilla groups began their truce six weeks after the IRA's ceasefire. But the Loyalist ceasefire has become more unstable as IRA fighters step up their campaign of violence.

Loyalists are thought to have been behind a failed bomb attack on Sinn Fein premises in the Irish Republic town of Monaghan two weeks ago as a reprisal for the IRA's killing of a British soldier in Northern Ireland last month.

Ervine, a leader of the Progressive Unionist Party, was speaking at Belfast International Airport before he and politicians in the Ulster Democratic Party (UDP), which is also linked to banned guerrillas, left for a visit to Washington coinciding with St Patrick's Day on Monday.
